name: Site enhancement oil (Synthol)

angle.text: Bodybuilders inject oil into lagging muscles such as biceps and delts to make them look bigger or reshape them. The size change is visible straight away and comes from the oil volume, not new muscle tissue.

summary: Oil injected straight into muscle to make it look bigger; case reports document embolism, granulomas, nerve damage and infection.
note: Medical literature documents serious complications including pulmonary oil embolism and stroke; no clinical trials exist.
currentQuick:
Site enhancement oil (SEO), best known by the brand name Synthol, is an oily liquid injected into muscle to increase its apparent size or alter its shape. It has been associated mainly with bodybuilders who use it on lagging or disproportionate muscles, a practice called fluffing [1].
The injected oil does not build muscle tissue; it sits in the muscle as a deposit. Medical case reports describe a range of complications, and the wiki found no clinical trials of its use.
How it works: Wikipedia reports a Synthol formulation of about 85% oil, 7.5% lidocaine and 7.5% alcohol, with sesame oil commonly used; some people instead inject poly(methyl methacrylate) or paraffin oil [1]. The material distends the muscle mechanically. A Sunday Times report cited in Wikipedia says injected muscle is not truly developed and may droop under gravity [1].
Risks and caveats: Reported complications include pulmonary embolism, nerve damage, infection, sclerosing lipogranuloma, stroke, oil-filled granulomas, cysts and ulcers, and allergic vasculitis from sesame oil; a 2011 case study reported multi-organ dysfunction in a user of multiple substances [1]. Wikipedia says synthol is not restricted and is sold online, while PMMA for muscle shaping is prohibited in the US [1].
deepLead:
Site enhancement oil (SEO), often called Synthol, santol or by the practice name "fluffing," is oil injected into muscle to increase its size or change its shape .
It is discussed as a hardmaxx or bodybuilding practice, mostly among competitive and professional bodybuilders who inject disproportionate or lagging muscles . It adds volume without adding contractile muscle tissue.
The published record consists largely of case reports and short articles documenting complications. No clinical trials of site enhancement oil have been found.

name: Progressive overload hypertrophy training

angle.text: Lifters use progressive overload as the core method for building a bigger physique, adding weight or reps over time. It is widely taught in strength science, with the best ways to progress still debated.

summary: The principle of steadily increasing load, reps or volume to keep muscles adapting; widely taught in strength science, with the details of how best to progress still debated.
note: Excess training can cause overtraining, which periodization is used to manage.
currentQuick:
Progressive overload means gradually increasing the demand placed on muscles over time, by adding weight, repetitions, sets or other stress, so they keep adapting and growing. It is a standard principle in strength and hypertrophy training and is discussed in lifting communities as the basis of getting bigger.
Research summarised by encyclopedias links hypertrophy to mechanical tension, total training volume and progressive overload, while the best way to apply the principle is still studied.
How it works: Resistance training under greater-than-normal demand triggers adaptation: neural changes first, then increases in muscle mass and connective-tissue strength [1]. Mechanical tension is the currently accepted theory of hypertrophy, activating mTOR signaling and muscle protein synthesis, though exact mechanisms are not fully understood [2].
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia notes that excessive training can cause overtraining and that periodization is used to help prevent it [1]. Injury risk depends on technique, load and individual factors, which the cited encyclopedia entries do not quantify.
deepLead:
Progressive overload is a training principle in which the stress placed on the musculoskeletal and nervous systems is gradually increased so that strength and muscle mass continue to develop .
In looksmaxxing and lifting communities it is treated as the core of muscle-building for physique, and it underlies discussions of routines, splits and periodization. The concept is long established in exercise science and is cited in guidelines such as those of the American College of Sports Medicine .
Evidence broadly supports the principle that training volume and progressive overload relate to hypertrophy; how much to progress, and by which variable, is still examined in research .

name: Push/pull/legs (PPL)

angle.text: A popular weekly split among lifters aiming to build a muscular physique with each muscle trained about twice a week. No cited research ranks it above other splits.

summary: A three-way weekly training split (pushing muscles, pulling muscles, legs); popular in lifting circles, and no cited research ranks it above other splits.
note: Encyclopedic sources cite no comparative research on training splits.
currentQuick:
Push/pull/legs, or PPL, is a way of dividing weekly weight training into sessions: one for pushing movements and muscles, one for pulling, and one for legs. It is one of several common split types alongside full-body, upper/lower and the bro split [1].
It is commonly discussed in lifting and looksmaxxing communities as a structure for building physique. Wikipedia's section on splits is tagged as needing a better source and cites no comparative research [1].
How it works: A split distributes weekly training volume across muscle groups and days [1]. Research summarised on Wikipedia reports that with equalized volume, training frequency did not influence strength, and for muscle growth two sessions per week produced greater effects than one [1]. How these findings apply to PPL specifically is not stated in the sources.
Risks and caveats: No harms specific to PPL are documented in the sources consulted. General resistance-training cautions apply, such as overtraining from excessive volume [2].
deepLead:
Push/pull/legs (PPL) is a training split that divides weekly resistance training into push, pull and leg days. Wikipedia defines a split as how a trainee divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days, and lists push/pull/legs among common splits .
The wiki treats it as a routine structure popular in lifting communities. The structure itself is documented only briefly in encyclopedias, and no comparative studies of splits are cited there .
Research summarised alongside it concerns frequency and volume in general, which are the variables a split changes.

name: Bro split

angle.text: A classic bodybuilding routine used to build size by hitting one muscle group hard each day. It is widely used in gym culture, and no cited research ranks it against other splits.

summary: A weekly routine that trains one muscle group per day; widely used in bodybuilding culture, with no cited research ranking it against other splits.
note: Encyclopedic sources cite no comparative research on training splits; the frequency research summarised there concerns muscle groups trained twice weekly versus once.
currentQuick:
The bro split is a way of organising weight training in which each session focuses on one muscle group, for example chest one day, back another, then shoulders, arms and legs. Wikipedia lists it among the common splits alongside full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs [1].
It is associated with bodybuilding culture and is discussed in lifting forums as a classic arrangement. The wiki found no comparative studies of splits in the sources reviewed.
How it works: A split divides weekly training volume across muscle groups and days [1]. In a bro split each muscle group is typically trained directly about once per week. Wikipedia's summary of frequency research says two sessions per week produced greater muscle growth than one, while strength gains were not influenced by frequency when total volume was equal [1][2].
Risks and caveats: No harms specific to the bro split are documented in the sources consulted. General resistance-training cautions, such as overtraining with excessive volume, apply [3].
deepLead:
The bro split is a weekly training split in which different muscle groups are trained on separate days, typically one group per session. Wikipedia names it as one of the common splits, along with full body, upper/lower and push/pull/legs .
The name is slang from lifting communities. Encyclopedic coverage is brief and the split section is flagged as needing a better source; no comparative research on splits is cited .
The relevant research concerns training frequency and volume in general: for muscle growth, two sessions per week per muscle group produced greater effects than one, whereas with equal volume frequency did not influence strength .

name: Beginner strength programs (5x5, SS, GZCLP)

angle.text: Beginners follow these barbell programs to add size and strength quickly with a few compound lifts. Their appeal rests on coaching lore and widespread use; no head-to-head trials compare them.

summary: Linear-progression barbell routines that beginners use to add size and strength, with plenty of coaching lore and no head-to-head trials.
note: Sources describe the programs and authors but not trials of the named templates.
currentQuick:
Beginner strength programs such as 5x5, Starting Strength and GZCLP are barbell routines in which a new lifter repeats a few compound lifts and adds a little weight each session. They are the usual starting recommendation in lifting and looksmaxxing communities for building muscle.
The programs come from coaches' books and websites. The research literature supports progressive resistance training in general, but no trials were found comparing the named programs.
How it works: Lifters repeat squats, presses and deadlifts several times a week and increase load in small steps. Authors say novices recover fast enough that this steady increase drives early strength and size gains.
Risks and caveats: Heavy barbell lifting carries the usual risks of resistance training, mainly from poor technique or rapid load increases. No program-specific injury data were identified.
deepLead:
Beginner strength programs are structured barbell routines built around a few compound lifts, such as the squat, bench press, overhead press and deadlift, in which the load is increased by a small fixed amount at each session or week. This approach is usually called linear progression. Three names are most often used in lifting communities: 5x5 (five sets of five repetitions, including the StrongLifts variant), Starting Strength (often abbreviated SS, from Mark Rippetoe's book), and GZCLP (a tiered linear-progression template shared online).
In looksmaxxing communities these programs are discussed as the default entry point for building muscle mass, which proponents say improves frame, posture and overall physical presentation. Starting Strength centres on the squat, deadlift, press, bench press and power clean, with a small number of assistance exercises . Mark Rippetoe, a former powerlifter and gym owner, co-authored the first edition of the book with Lon Kilgore in 2005 .
Encyclopedic sources describe the programs and their authors but do not summarise controlled trials of these specific named routines. The wider research literature on resistance training supports progressive overload and adequate volume as drivers of strength and muscle growth, but head-to-head trials of branded beginner programs are not documented in the sources used for this article .

name: High intensity training (HIT / Mentzer)

chain: One or few sets to failure
angle.text: Followers of Mentzer's Heavy Duty use brief, infrequent sessions taken to failure to build muscle. It is famous in bodybuilding history, while the full system has not been tested as a whole.

summary: Mentzer's Heavy Duty: one or few sets to failure with long rests, famous in bodybuilding history, untested as a complete system.
note: Advocates disagree on details; no trials of the full Mentzer protocol were identified.
currentQuick:
High-intensity training uses short, infrequent workouts taken to muscular failure. Arthur Jones popularised it in the 1970s, and bodybuilder Mike Mentzer developed the Heavy Duty version with very few sets and long recovery.
Followers say effort, not volume, drives muscle growth. Critics say it departs from conventional guidance, and no trials of the complete Mentzer system were found.
How it works: Each set is pushed to momentary failure with slow, strict form, then the muscle is given several days to recover before the next session.
Risks and caveats: Training to failure carries the general risks of resistance training, including fatigue and injury if form breaks down. No program-specific harm data were identified.
deepLead:
High-intensity training (HIT) is a strength-training method centred on brief, infrequent workouts in which each set is taken to momentary muscular failure. It was popularised in the 1970s by Arthur Jones, founder of Nautilus . Mike Mentzer, an American professional bodybuilder, later developed his own version called Heavy Duty, which used very few sets and long recovery periods .
Within appearance and physique communities, HIT is discussed as a time-efficient route to muscle size. Proponents argue that hypertrophy depends on intensity of effort rather than the amount of work, while critics of the method dispute its claims and its departure from conventional guidance .
The encyclopedic sources consulted describe the history and principles of HIT but do not summarise controlled trials of Mentzer's specific system.

name: Renaissance Periodization (RP) volume training

chain: Stay between minimum and max volume
angle.text: Lifters use the MEV, MAV and MRV framework to choose how many weekly sets to do for each muscle to grow. It is popular in lifting circles, with no independent trial of the system itself.

summary: Israetel's MEV/MAV/MRV set-count framework: popular in lifting circles, with no independent trial of the system itself.
note: Figures come largely from RP's own and affiliated material.
currentQuick:
Renaissance Periodization is a coaching company founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw. Its best-known idea is a set of weekly volume landmarks: minimum effective, maximum adaptive and maximum recoverable volume.
The framework is widely discussed among lifters. Independent efficacy studies of the full system were not found.
How it works: Trainees begin at a low weekly set count per muscle and add sets over a training block as recovery allows, then reduce volume before repeating.
Risks and caveats: Higher volumes carry general overuse and fatigue risks of resistance training. Critics mention cost and some diet recommendations; no system-specific harm data were identified.
deepLead:
Renaissance Periodization (RP) is a fitness company co-founded in 2012 by Mike Israetel and Nick Shaw . It is associated with a volume-management framework for muscle building built around three weekly set benchmarks: minimum effective volume (MEV), maximum adaptive volume (MAV) and maximum recoverable volume (MRV) .
Israetel is an American exercise scientist and bodybuilder with a PhD in sports physiology . RP offers coaching, apps, courses and ebooks, and the volume landmarks are popular in lifting communities as a way to plan how many sets to do per muscle each week .
No independent trials of the RP system as a whole were identified in the sources consulted, and one encyclopedic source states that no large-scale independent efficacy studies were found .

name: Blood flow restriction (BFR) training

chain: Muscle gain with less joint stress
angle.text: Users wrap cuffs on arms or legs to build muscle with light weights, and some forum posters pair it with claims of height gain. The muscle use has a real rehab research base; the height claims have no study behind them.

summary: Cuff-assisted light-load lifting with a real rehab research base; the height-growth versions on forums have no study behind them.
note: On looksmaxxing forums BFR often means buccal fat removal; this entry is the exercise method.
currentQuick:
Blood flow restriction training uses a cuff on the arm or thigh to partly limit blood flow during light exercise. It originated in Japan in the 1960s as KAATSU and is now studied in rehabilitation and sport.
Meta-analyses report strength and muscle-size gains from low-load BFR, with varied results across groups. Forum claims about height growth have not been tested.
How it works: The cuff mainly restricts blood leaving the muscle, creating a low-oxygen, metabolite-rich state that researchers think signals growth even at light loads.
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include numbness, soreness and bruising; rare serious events like rhabdomyolysis and thrombosis are described, especially with improvised straps. Clotting disorders and peripheral artery disease are listed contraindications.
deepLead:
Blood flow restriction (BFR) training is a method in which a cuff or band placed on the upper arm or thigh partly restricts blood flow while a person exercises with light loads. It was developed by Dr. Yoshiaki Sato in Japan in 1966, where it is known as KAATSU .
Research on BFR is substantial in rehabilitation and sports science. A 2012 meta-analysis and later reviews examine whether low-load exercise with restriction can produce strength and size gains . A position stand on methodology and safety was published in 2019 .
Note on terminology: in looksmaxxing forums the abbreviation BFR more often refers to buccal fat removal, a facial surgery, and the same threads sometimes discuss BFR training under the same acronym. This article covers the exercise method.

name: Lengthened partials / stretch training

angle.text: Lifters train only the stretched part of a rep, such as the bottom of a curl or fly, to build more muscle in that muscle. It is plausible in hypertrophy theory and thinly documented so far.

summary: Overloading only the stretched part of a rep; plausible in hypertrophy theory, thinly documented here.
note: Thin sources; no dedicated trials summarised.
currentQuick:
Lengthened partials are repetitions done only in the stretched portion of a lift. Lifters use them to load muscles at long lengths.
Hypertrophy overviews describe training at long muscle lengths as beneficial, but no dedicated trials were summarised here.
How it works: The technique aims to keep mechanical tension high while the muscle is elongated, which proponents link to growth.
Risks and caveats: Heavy loading in stretched positions can stress joints and connective tissue, as with other resistance training. No technique-specific harm data were identified.
deepLead:
Lengthened partials are repetitions performed only through the stretched portion of an exercise's range of motion, for example the bottom half of a curl or fly, rather than the full range. They are discussed in lifting communities as a way to emphasise the position in which the muscle is most elongated.
A general-purpose encyclopedic account of hypertrophy reports that full range of motion, especially at elongated muscle lengths, is described as enhancing growth more than partial range, and that partial-range training at longer muscle lengths is also said to promote hypertrophy, possibly through muscle damage .
The sources consulted for this entry do not summarise dedicated trials of lengthened partials.

name: Myo-reps / drop sets

chain: Extra hard reps in less time
angle.text: Lifters use drop sets and myo-reps to pack more hard reps into less time for muscle growth. Drop sets have a long history, while myo-reps have only recently been trialled.

summary: Time-saving to-failure set techniques; drop sets have a long history, myo-reps are newer and only just trialled.
note: Few trials; findings are mixed.
currentQuick:
Drop sets keep exercising with lighter weight after failure at a heavier one. Myo-reps use an activation set followed by short mini-sets with brief rests.
Summaries report possible extra muscle growth from drop sets but mixed findings, and myo-reps have only recently been trialled against straight sets.
How it works: Both methods keep a muscle working near failure for more total repetitions in a short time, which advocates say raises the growth stimulus per minute.
Risks and caveats: Working to failure adds fatigue and soreness; general resistance-training injury risks apply. No technique-specific harm data were identified.
deepLead:
Drop sets and myo-reps are resistance-training intensity techniques meant to pack more hard repetitions into less time. A drop set continues exercising with a lighter weight after reaching muscle failure at a heavier one . Myo-reps are a related method in which a lifter performs an initial high-effort set and then several short mini-sets with brief rests; a 2026 trial compared the approach with traditional straight sets in resistance-trained men .
Drop sets have a longer documented history: Henry Atkins, editor of Body Culture magazine, described the approach in the late 1940s as the multi-poundage system, and drop sets were part of Joe Weider's Weider System in the 1980s . Encyclopedic coverage says drop sets may increase muscle growth more than traditional three-set training, while some researchers report mixed or inconclusive findings .

name: Shoulder-width training (lateral raises, delts)

angle.text: Users train the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the shoulders look wider and improve frame proportions. Forum members post bideltoid measurements and compare them against height. Muscle growth is well established; its effect on rated attractiveness is based on anecdote.

summary: Building the side delts, mostly with lateral raises, to make the frame look wider; muscle can change visible width but not bone width.
note: Muscle adds visible shoulder width; skeletal (clavicle) width is not changed by training.
currentQuick:
Shoulder-width training is the looksmaxxing practice of growing the deltoid muscles, especially the side (lateral) heads, so the shoulders look broader. The usual tool is the lateral raise, an arm-abduction exercise.
Community members discuss it as a way to improve upper-body proportions, often alongside the V-taper idea. They also trade bideltoid measurements in inches and compare them to height.
How it works: The deltoid has three heads that run from the clavicle and shoulder blade to the upper arm, and the middle fibers are best placed to lift the arm out to the side. Growing that muscle adds soft-tissue thickness at the sides of the shoulder, which increases the measured and apparent width. The underlying bone structure stays as it is.
Risks and caveats: Lifting carries ordinary training risks such as shoulder strain. Forum users joke about rotator cuff damage from very high volume. No studies were found that test shoulder-width training for appearance or attractiveness.
deepLead:
Shoulder-width training is a looksmaxxing practice in which people train the deltoid muscles, most often with lateral raises, to make the shoulders appear wider. It is discussed in the looksmax.org community as part of improving frame and proportions, and members regularly post their "bideltoid" measurements and ask how they compare with the general population at a given height .
Anatomically, the deltoid has anterior, intermediate (lateral) and posterior heads, and the intermediate fibers are the best positioned to abduct the arm, which is the movement a lateral raise trains . Proponents say that developing this muscle adds visible breadth at the top of the torso.
No clinical studies of shoulder-width training as an appearance intervention were found. A small body of attractiveness research examines male shoulder dimensions and perceived attractiveness in general, but it does not test training programs .

name: V-taper / shoulder-to-waist ratio

angle.text: Lifters and looksmaxxers aim for a shoulder-to-waist ratio near 1.6 by building the shoulders and back while cutting waist fat. The ratio is a bodybuilding ideal, and the 1.6 target is forum-quoted rather than drawn from a specific attractiveness study.

summary: The broad-shoulders, narrow-waist silhouette that lifters and looksmaxxers treat as the male physique ideal, usually quoted as a ratio near 1.6.
note: The 1.6 'golden ratio' target comes from bodybuilding culture; research on male body shape and attractiveness is limited.
currentQuick:
A V-taper is a torso that is wide at the shoulders and upper back and narrows to a small waist. In bodybuilding it is a classic ideal, and in looksmaxxing it is a standard frame goal often written as a shoulder-to-waist ratio.
A figure of about 1.6, tied to the golden ratio, is commonly cited as the target. Community members discuss how to approach it through delt and lat training and fat loss.
How it works: The ratio rises when the shoulders and upper back get wider or the waist gets smaller. Wider means deltoid and latissimus muscle growth on top of the bone structure set by the clavicles. Smaller waist is mainly linked to body fat loss; abdominal exercise on its own is described as insufficient for reducing waist girth.
Risks and caveats: The practice itself is ordinary training and dieting. Reported concerns are mostly about body-image fixation and about skipping legs or overtraining while chasing a number. The 1.6 target is a cultural convention, and the research behind it is thin.
deepLead:
The V-taper is a physique in which broad shoulders and a wide upper back narrow down to a slim waist, giving an inverted-triangle silhouette. It is a long-standing ideal in bodybuilding and is discussed in looksmaxxing as the shoulder-to-waist ratio .
A figure of about 1.6, linked to the golden ratio, is often stated as the target. Grokipedia, an AI-generated source, attributes this to bodybuilding aesthetics and credits figures such as Steve Reeves and Arnold Schwarzenegger with popularizing the look, although several of its citations for the attractiveness claims do not appear to match those claims .
Wikipedia's article on waist-hip ratio, which is about attractiveness research, reports one study in which the waist-to-chest ratio was the largest determinant of male attractiveness, and does not discuss shoulder-to-waist ratio itself . No clinical studies of the ratio as a target were found.

name: Biacromial / clavicle width

angle.text: Looksmaxxers treat biacromial and clavicle width as the fixed skeletal base that muscle can add to but not change. Specific bideltoid numbers are quoted as marks of a high-status frame, a belief from forum discussion rather than studied thresholds.

summary: The bone-based width of the shoulder girdle, which looksmaxxers treat as a fixed frame limit that muscle can only add to.
note: Mostly a measurement concept; no studies found on appearance effects.
currentQuick:
Biacromial width is the distance between the outer points of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length is the length of the collarbones. Looksmaxxers treat both as the skeletal limit on how wide the shoulders can look.
Community threads ask what counts as a good clavicle or bideltoid width and compare measurements, often in inches and at a stated height.
How it works: The clavicle is a horizontal strut between the sternum and shoulder blade. Males usually have longer clavicles than females, and the bone finishes ossifying around age 21 to 25. Muscle such as the deltoids sits on top of this frame and adds soft-tissue width.
Risks and caveats: Measuring is harmless, though community comparison can feed body-image concern. Surgery to alter the clavicle is a separate topic with its own risks, covered in the clavicle lengthening osteotomy article.
deepLead:
Biacromial width, the span across the acromion processes of the shoulder blades, and clavicle length are discussed in looksmaxxing as the bone-set limits on shoulder width. Members commonly say that training can add muscle on the outside of this frame but cannot change the skeleton .
Wikipedia describes the clavicle as an S-shaped long bone lying horizontally between shoulder blade and sternum. It reports that males usually have longer and larger clavicles than females, and that the bone begins ossifying very early in fetal life but finishes only around age 21 to 25 .
No clinical studies of biacromial or clavicle width as an attractiveness or looksmaxxing target were found.

name: Clavicle lengthening osteotomy

angle.text: Discussed in hardmaxxing circles as an extreme surgery to widen the shoulders by lengthening the collarbones. It is raised as a rare option and is not an established cosmetic operation; no cosmetic studies were found.

summary: A rare, extreme surgery floated on forums to widen the shoulders by cutting and lengthening the collarbones; no cosmetic studies found.
note: No published trials of the operation for cosmetic shoulder widening were found.
currentQuick:
Clavicle lengthening osteotomy is a surgical idea in which a collarbone is cut and lengthened to widen the shoulders. In looksmaxxing it is described as an extreme, rarely performed hardmaxxing option.
No clinical studies of the operation for appearance were found. Surgical literature on the clavicle mostly covers fractures, non-union and malunion.
How it works: An osteotomy is a surgical cut through bone. Applied to the clavicle, the goal would be to increase bone length and so shoulder breadth. Related operations in the literature treat painful non-union and malunion after fractures.
Risks and caveats: Clavicle surgery sits close to nerves and vessels. A published case series of operations for late fracture complications mentions conditions such as thoracic outlet syndrome and brachial plexus neuroma among the problems treated. Anesthesia for clavicle surgery often involves nerve blocks that can affect breathing muscles.
deepLead:
Clavicle lengthening osteotomy refers to a surgical procedure in which the collarbone is cut and lengthened with the aim of widening the shoulders. It appears in looksmaxxing circles as a rare, extreme hardmaxxing option and is not an established cosmetic operation.
No studies or trials of clavicle lengthening for cosmetic shoulder widening were found. The surgical literature on the clavicle concerns fractures and their complications. One case series described operative treatment of late complications of clavicle fractures, including painful non-union, malunion and neurogenic or vascular thoracic outlet syndrome .
Registered clinical trials on the clavicle found in the sources are about fracture treatment, plates and pins, not cosmetic lengthening .

name: Stomach vacuum / waist training

angle.text: Users practice the stomach vacuum to train the transversus abdominis and make the waist look smaller, supporting a V-taper. The muscle is well described anatomically; its use for waist appearance is based on anecdote with little research.

summary: Pulling the belly in to train the deep abdominal muscle for a smaller-looking waist; little research exists on it for appearance.
note: Sources on abdominal exercise say it does not by itself reduce abdominal fat.
currentQuick:
The stomach vacuum is an exercise in which the abdomen is drawn inward, aimed at the transversus abdominis, the deepest abdominal muscle. Forum users discuss it as a way to get a tighter-looking waist.
Sources are thin. A looksmax.org thread has a user asking whether others lost the ability to do it and reporting it came back with renewed training.
How it works: The transversus abdominis is one of four abdominal wall muscles. Wikipedia notes that whether training this deep core muscle specifically is worthwhile is disputed, and that abdominal exercise alone is not enough to reduce abdominal fat or girth according to a 2011 study.
Risks and caveats: No harms data were found for the exercise. Community talk of 'waist training' sometimes also refers to compression garments, which this entry does not cover.
deepLead:
The stomach vacuum is an abdominal exercise in which the stomach is pulled inward, discussed in looksmaxxing as a way to make the waist look smaller. It is associated with the transversus abdominis, the deepest of the four muscles of the front abdominal wall .
Community material is limited to short forum posts, such as a thread in which a user says he nearly lost the ability to perform it two years earlier and can do it easily again after resuming training . No clinical studies were found.

name: Neckmaxxing / neck training

angle.text: Neckmaxxers train the neck to make it thicker, believing this adds a masculine, dominant look and better face and frame proportions. Neck-to-jaw ratio targets circulate on forums, and no published study validates them.

summary: Building a thicker neck to improve frame and jaw proportions; discussed with ratio targets that no published study validates.
note: Community guides involve loaded neck exercises; ratio targets are forum conventions.
currentQuick:
Neckmaxxing is the practice of training the neck muscles to make the neck thicker, which proponents say improves overall proportions and the look of the jaw. It is described on looksmax.org as a softmaxx.
Forum posts propose ideal ratios, for example neck width compared with jaw (bigonial) width near 1:1, and share training guides.
How it works: Neck exercises load the muscles around the cervical spine, with the sternocleidomastoid named in forum guides as the muscle that thickens the neck from the front. Proponents say a thicker neck makes a narrow head and jaw look more balanced with the body.
Risks and caveats: Loaded neck exercises sit near the cervical spine. One forum guide calls neck work one of the most dangerous softmaxxes. No clinical studies of neckmaxxing for appearance were found.
deepLead:
Neckmaxxing is the looksmaxxing practice of training the neck to make it thicker, on the belief that a wider neck contributes to a masculine, dominant look and better facial and frame proportions .
Forum posts offer ideal ratios, such as a neck-to-bigonial (jaw width) ratio of roughly 0.95 to 1, and in one thread a neck width-to-height ratio near 1.35 . Another guide states the neck should match the width of the widest part of the face and that the bigonial to bizygomatic ratio should be around 0.9 to 1.05 . These are community conventions, and no published study validating them was found.
No clinical studies of neck training for appearance were found.

name: Grip and forearm training

angle.text: Lifters use wrist curls, hangs, carries and grippers to build forearm size and grip strength, valued for the look of the arms. Strength gains are well documented in sport; the claim that thick forearms look more attractive is anecdotal.

summary: Targeted work for the hands and forearms to build grip strength and forearm size; popular for the look of the arms, with little direct research on appearance.
note: Published trials mostly measure strength, endurance or sport performance rather than forearm appearance.
currentQuick:
Grip and forearm training is the deliberate exercising of the muscles that close the hand and move the wrist, usually with wrist curls, hangs, carries and similar movements. In looksmaxxing and physique circles it is discussed mainly because forearm size is a visible part of how the arms look.
A small number of published studies have tested forearm training programs, mostly in athletes or lab settings, and report gains in strength, endurance or muscle size. No published trial has tested whether forearm training changes how attractive someone is judged to look.
How it works: The forearm contains a front (flexor) group that flexes the wrist and fingers and a back (extensor) group that extends them, plus muscles that rotate the forearm and the brachioradialis, an elbow flexor. Training aims to load these muscles so they adapt, as other skeletal muscles do under resistance exercise.
Risks and caveats: Forearm training is generally low-risk exercise. Overuse of the wrist and elbow tendons is a general concern with repetitive loading, though the sources reviewed here do not quantify it for this practice. Claims about attractiveness are untested.
deepLead:
Grip and forearm training refers to exercise aimed at the muscles of the forearm and hand, which produce wrist movement and gripping force. Practitioners use movements such as wrist curls, dead hangs, loaded carries and gripper devices, and in strength sports grip is also treated as a performance factor in pulling lifts.
In looksmaxxing communities the topic is raised mainly for appearance: thick forearms are described by posters as part of a strong, masculine arm and wrist look. Related discussion concerns wrist circumference and bone structure, which proponents say training cannot change.
Published research on forearm training is sparse and mostly concerns function rather than looks. Studies include a 4-week unilateral forearm training trial that increased endurance time during rhythmic handgrip , 12-week wrist and forearm programs in high school baseball players , and a hybrid training method that reported increases in forearm strength and mass in healthy men . No study found examines perceived attractiveness.

name: Calisthenics / gymnast physique

angle.text: People use push-ups, pull-ups, dips and skills like levers to build a lean, muscular, gymnast-style body with little equipment. Bodyweight training is studied for strength and muscle; its aesthetic results specifically have limited direct evidence.

summary: Building a lean, muscular, gymnast-style frame through bodyweight training; popular as a low-cost route to size, with direct evidence on its aesthetic results limited.
note: Trials comparing calisthenics against weights for appearance are not found; calisthenics often appears only as a comparison arm in other studies.
currentQuick:
Calisthenics is strength training that uses body weight as resistance, with exercises such as push-ups, pull-ups, dips and squats, and advanced holds like the planche and front lever. The gymnast physique is the broad-shouldered, lean, muscular look associated with this style.
In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as an inexpensive way to build the upper body at home. Posters disagree about whether it matches weight training for muscle size, particularly for the legs.
How it works: Muscle is loaded by moving the body through harder variations, more repetitions or slower tempos (progressive overload). Proponents say this produces hypertrophy similar to weight training in beginners.
Risks and caveats: Calisthenics is generally low-cost and low-risk, though advanced skills place heavy loads on wrists, elbows and shoulders. Published research on this practice for appearance specifically is limited.
deepLead:
Calisthenics, also called bodyweight exercise, is strength training that uses the body's own weight for resistance and typically requires little or no equipment . Its name derives from Greek words for beauty and strength . Common exercises include push-ups, pull-ups, dips, squats and planks, while advanced skills include handstands, front and back levers, muscle-ups and the planche .
The 'gymnast physique' refers to the lean, muscular upper body, wide shoulders and narrow waist associated with competitive gymnasts and calisthenics athletes. In looksmaxxing communities, calisthenics is often raised as a low-budget route to this look, with posters sharing routines built around pull-ups, chin-ups, push-ups and squats .
No published trial found tests calisthenics for physique or perceived attractiveness. Related research uses calisthenics mainly as a comparison arm in other trials .

name: Ring training / planche progressions

angle.text: Practitioners use ring dips, levers and planche progressions as a skill-based route to upper-body size and a gymnast look. The gymnast build is the draw; no studies on appearance outcomes were found.

summary: Gymnastic-style strength work on rings and planche holds; a skill-based route to upper-body size with no appearance studies behind it.
note: Little published research on appearance outcomes; advanced straight-arm skills load the wrists, elbows and shoulders heavily.
currentQuick:
Ring training uses suspended gymnastic rings for push, pull and hold exercises, and the planche is a straight-arm hold with the body horizontal above the hands. Both come from gymnastics and calisthenics.
They are discussed in physique culture as a route to a gymnast-style upper body. Little research exists on the practice, and none on appearance outcomes.
How it works: Rings are unstable, so the body must control the movement as well as lift it. Progressions move from easier variations toward the full skill by adjusting leverage.
Risks and caveats: Advanced static holds load the wrists, elbows and shoulders heavily. This article does not cover technique.
deepLead:
Gymnastic rings are two rings hung from a frame by straps, used in men's artistic gymnastics. A standard apparatus has rings with an 18 cm inner diameter hung 300 cm from the attachment point . Elements include strength holds such as the iron cross and Maltese cross, and swing elements such as giant swings .
The planche is a calisthenics static hold in which the body is held parallel to the floor supported on the arms; Wikipedia's calisthenics article describes it as the most advanced of the common skills, often reached only after years of training . Both skills are also grouped under statics, the isometric holds in calisthenics .
Within physique communities these skills are discussed as part of the gymnast look. No published study found tests ring or planche training for appearance outcomes.

name: Dirty bulk / lean bulk

chain: More size, then cut to reveal it
angle.text: Lifters eat in a surplus to gain muscle, either a large loosely tracked one (dirty bulk) or a small controlled one (lean bulk), usually followed by a cut. Bulking and cutting come from bodybuilding practice; the relative merits of each style are debated by forum posters.

summary: Two ways of eating in a calorie surplus to gain size: a large, loosely tracked surplus versus a small, controlled one.
note: Wikipedia describes dirty bulking as likely to add significant fat and as carrying cardiovascular and insulin-related concerns; forum debates are mostly anecdotal.
currentQuick:
Bulking means eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle. A lean (or clean) bulk uses a small surplus with tracking to limit fat gain, while a dirty bulk uses a large surplus with little tracking, often including processed foods.
On looksmax.org, younger and thinner users ask which approach avoids looking soft or bloated while gaining size. Responses range from small planned surpluses to long continuous bulks.
How it works: A surplus supplies energy for tissue growth. Wikipedia says a sustained surplus can add more lean mass than eating at maintenance, with some fat gain expected, and that a larger surplus or longer bulk adds more fat.
Risks and caveats: Wikipedia describes dirty bulking as producing fast gain but usually significant fat, followed by a harsher cut, with long-term concerns for cardiovascular health and insulin sensitivity. Forum users also report fear of looking fat or bloated.
deepLead:
Bulking is the bodybuilding practice of eating in a calorie surplus to build muscle, usually followed by a cutting phase in a deficit . Wikipedia says competitive bodybuilders spend most of the year in an off-season build and cut for roughly 12 to 14 weeks before a contest .
Clean or lean bulking is described as trying to increase muscle without fat gain, using tracking and a controlled surplus, while dirty bulking is a large untracked surplus that can include junk food, giving faster weight gain but usually more fat .
On looksmax.org the topic appears as questions from users who want size without looking chubby or bloated . No published trial found tests clean versus dirty bulking for appearance outcomes.
